967.title: Cyril, Methodius and Valentine (14 February)
967.hook: the calendar keeps the brothers of the Slavs on the same day as Valentine, a Roman martyr
967.howItsDone: Catholics in the Roman calendar keep 14 February as the memorial of Saints Cyril and Methodius, patrons of Europe, while Valentine is remembered in the Roman Martyrology; Slavic Catholic and Orthodox communities celebrate the brothers with special honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Apollonia of Alexandria, the older woman who would not deny Christ before a mob. Your line was she kept faith. Did a dentist get a thank-you? Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

Shop windows on the fourteenth of February: red hearts, roses in plastic sleeves, cards with a little winged boy and his bow. Open the Church's calendar to the same square, though, and the first names printed there are two brothers from the Greek world who gave a people an alphabet. Cyril and Methodius. Somewhere below them, in the old list of martyrs, is a Roman called Valentine. So the day holds two kinds of gift side by side. One is love. The other is letters. Today is about the brothers, and the man who shares their day.
screen: `HEARTS IN THE SHOP WINDOW.` → `TWO BROTHERS IN THE CALENDAR.` → `LOVE, AND LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Start with the brothers. Tradition says they grew up in Thessalonica, in Greece, and that they were sent north to the Slavic peoples, who had no written form of their own language. Preaching to someone in a borrowed language is like singing them a song in a key they can't reach. So the brothers did something patient and strange: they built an alphabet. With it they translated the Gospels and the prayers of the liturgy into the people's own Slavonic speech. Not everyone liked it. Tradition says some churchmen argued that worship belonged only in the old sacred languages, and the brothers traveled to Rome to make their case, and the pope received them and let the Slavonic books be used. Cyril, the younger, died in Rome. Methodius went back and kept working. There's a line in the Acts of the Apostles, from Pentecost, that sounds like their whole life. In the Douay-Rheims, the crowd says: "we have heard them speak in our own tongues the wonderful works of God." That was the brothers' hope for every Slavic village. The Church remembers them as apostles of the Slavs and keeps them among the patron saints of Europe. And Valentine? The honest answer is that very little is known. He is remembered as a Roman martyr. The hearts, the cards and the birds pairing off came later, from customs and poems, not from anything we know of his life. Love and letters. The Church sets them on one day, and they belong together: to give someone words in their own language is a way of loving them.
screen: `A PEOPLE WITHOUT A WRITTEN LANGUAGE.` · `TWO BROTHERS BUILD AN ALPHABET.` · `ROME LETS THE SLAVONIC BOOKS BE USED.` · `VALENTINE: A MARTYR WE KNOW LITTLE OF.` · then, large: `IN OUR OWN TONGUES THE WONDERFUL WORKS OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show love for someone in their own language. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind. Not a grand gesture, just one person. Then ask: what is their language? Some people hear love in words, some in a cooked meal, some in a fixed bike, some in a message that just says thinking of you. Choose the thing they'd understand, not the thing that's easiest for you to give. If you pray, you can hold that person before God for a moment. If you don't, just keep their face in mind and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Cyril. With his brother Methodius, the apostle of the Slavs, who gave a people letters for their own language so they could hear the Gospel in it.
Your line: love and letters. Today, learn to say thank you or good morning in the first language of someone you know, and use it on them. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

968.title: The martyrs of Libya (15 February)
968.hook: Coptic Christians killed on a beach in Libya, now honored in the Roman Martyrology
968.howItsDone: The Coptic Orthodox Church keeps these men as martyrs and saints on 15 February, and since their inclusion in the Roman Martyrology Catholics also remember them that day, often praying for Christians who suffer for their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyril and his brother Methodius, who built an alphabet so a people could hear the Gospel in their own tongue. Your line was love and letters. Who got a note from you? Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

The saints of the last few days lived long ago, in stories handed down. Today's saints were workers, in our own time. Men who had left their villages in Egypt to find jobs in Libya, to send money home to their families. They were kidnapped by an armed group, dressed in orange, led onto a beach by the sea, and killed. Their killers filmed it and sent the film around the world. Reports of the film say that, at the end, some of the men were heard calling on Jesus. The Church remembers them as the martyrs of Libya, and has a short name for them too.
screen: `WORKERS FAR FROM HOME.` → `A BEACH, AND A FILM.` → `CALLING ON JESUS.`

segments.voice: The men were, almost all of them, Coptic Orthodox Christians, from the ancient Church of Egypt. One man who died with them was from Ghana, and tradition among the Copts holds that he chose to stand with the others. Here's what makes this day unusual in a Catholic calendar. The Coptic Orthodox Church is not in full communion with Rome. They have their own pope in Alexandria, their own liturgy, their own saints. Their pope declared these men martyrs and saints of his Church. Later, Pope Francis received the Coptic pope at the Vatican and announced that the men would be added to the Roman Martyrology, the Catholic Church's official list of saints and martyrs. A Church honoring martyrs who were not its own members, because of how they died. Pope Francis had a phrase for this: an ecumenism of blood. Those who kill Christians, he said in effect, do not stop to ask which church they belong to. Catholics and Copts still differ on real questions, and both say so. But in the Martyrology, the names stand together. In the Greek of the Acts of the Apostles, the word for witnesses is the word English borrowed as martyr. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his followers, "you shall be witnesses unto me," and he sends that witness out to the uttermost part of the earth. A beach in Libya is one of those far places. These men did not preach a sermon there. Their witness was a name on their lips.
screen: `COPTIC CHRISTIANS FROM EGYPT.` · `A CHURCH NOT IN FULL COMMUNION WITH ROME.` · `ADDED TO THE ROMAN MARTYROLOGY.` · `AN ECUMENISM OF BLOOD.` · then, large: `YOU SHALL BE WITNESSES UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for, or remember, Coptic Christians. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the families in those villages, who sent their sons out to work and waited for money and calls that stopped coming. Then widen it: Coptic Christians today, in Egypt and in cities all over the world, getting up for church, raising children, burying their dead. If you pray, you can hold them before God in your own words, or with the Lord's Prayer. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, one breath for the families, one for the men. The bell holds the time.
The martyrs of Libya. Coptic Christians killed on a Libyan beach, declared saints by their own Church and added to the Catholic Martyrology.
Your line: the twenty-one. Today, learn one thing about a church or a faith other than your own, and keep it with respect. Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

969.title: Jacinta and Francisco Marto (20 February)
969.hook: two of the Fatima children, a brother and sister who died young and were canonized together
969.howItsDone: Catholics keep 20 February as the memorial of Saints Francisco and Jacinta Marto, especially in Portugal, and pilgrims visit their tombs at the shrine of Fatima, often praying the rosary there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the martyrs of Libya, Coptic workers whose names now stand in the Roman Martyrology. Your line was the twenty-one. What did you learn about a church that isn't yours? Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

A hillside in Portugal, sheep grazing, three children with a packed lunch and a long afternoon. Lucia, the oldest, and her two younger cousins, a brother and sister named Francisco and Jacinta Marto. They are supposed to say the rosary while they watch the flock, and, by Lucia's own later account, they sometimes rushed it, saying just the first words of each prayer so they could get back to their games. Then, the children said, a lady brighter than the sun appeared to them above a small tree. Today is about the brother and sister, and what happened to them after.
screen: `THREE CHILDREN AND A FLOCK.` → `A RUSHED ROSARY.` → `A LADY ABOVE A SMALL TREE.`

segments.voice: Fatima is famous for the visions: a lady the children understood to be Mary, messages about prayer and penance, a crowd watching the sky. The Church judged those events worthy of belief, which is the careful phrase it uses. Private revelations like Fatima are not part of the faith Catholics are required to hold, and Catholics are free to weigh them. But that is not why Jacinta and Francisco are saints. The Church canonizes people for the way they lived. And these two lived differently afterward. Francisco was the quiet one. Lucia remembered that he would slip into the parish church and sit near the tabernacle for hours, to keep company with the hidden Jesus, as he called him. He wanted, he said, to console God. Jacinta was the fierce one. She took the call to penance seriously, giving her lunch to poorer children, and offering up small hardships for sinners. Not long after the visions, both children fell seriously ill. Francisco died at home. Jacinta died in a hospital in Lisbon, far from her family. They were still children. Pope Francis canonized them together at Fatima. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus prays: "thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones." The Church, in naming these two, took him at his word. Holiness was not waiting for them to grow up.
screen: `THE VISIONS: WORTHY OF BELIEF, NOT REQUIRED.` · `SAINTS FOR HOW THEY LIVED.` · `FRANCISCO CONSOLES, JACINTA OFFERS.` · `TWO CHILDREN, SICK AND DYING.` · then, large: `REVEALED THEM TO LITTLE ONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for, or hold in mind, sick children. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a child you know who is unwell, or the children in a hospital near you tonight, and the parents sitting beside the beds, and the nurses on the late shift. You don't need words. Just keep them company, the way Francisco sat with the hidden Jesus. If you pray, you can offer them to God, perhaps with a Hail Mary. If you don't, give each one a slow breath. The bell holds the time.
Jacinta and Francisco Marto. A sister and brother from Fatima who died as children and were canonized for how they lived, not for what they saw.
Your line: the children of fatima. Today, notice a child's seriousness about something, and take it seriously too, without smiling it away. Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

970.title: Peter Damian (21 February)
970.hook: a monk and reformer who wrote blunt letters against corruption in the Church
970.howItsDone: Catholics keep 21 February as the memorial of Saint Peter Damian, bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his letters and writings on prayer are read in the Liturgy of the Hours and by those interested in Church reform.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jacinta and Francisco Marto, the children of Fatima, saints for how they lived. Your line was the children of fatima. Whose seriousness did you take seriously? Day nine hundred seventy.

Some letters you write three times. The first draft is furious. The second is so polite it says nothing. The third, if you're lucky, says the true thing plainly, because you care about the person reading it. Peter Damian spent much of his life writing the third kind. He was a monk in Italy who loved silence and his hermit's cell, and he kept being pulled out of it to tell bishops, priests and even popes what they did not want to hear. He signed himself, tradition says, Peter the sinner, monk. Today is about him, and about love that doesn't flatter.
screen: `THREE DRAFTS OF A HARD LETTER.` → `A MONK PULLED FROM HIS CELL.` → `PETER THE SINNER, MONK.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Peter Damian began poor. An orphan, he was taken in by relatives and set to work as a boy looking after pigs, until an older brother saw how bright he was and paid for his schooling. He became a teacher, then left it all for a hermitage, where the monks lived in small cells and prayed through the night. He would have stayed. But the Church of his day was sick in ways that were hard to miss. Church offices were being bought and sold, a corruption known as simony. Clergy were living double lives. Peter wrote about it, in letters that named things plainly, and the popes kept calling him to help with reform. He was made a cardinal and bishop, and, tradition says, asked more than once to be allowed to go back to his cell. What makes him worth remembering is not just that he was blunt. Plenty of people are blunt. It's that he aimed the same honesty at himself. That signature, Peter the sinner, was not a pose. The book of Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims, has a line for this kind of friend: "Better are the wounds of a friend, than the deceitful kisses of an enemy." Peter Damian's letters could wound. He wrote them because he loved the Church, not because he wanted to win. The Church later named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone. Blunt love tells the truth, includes itself in the problem, and stays to help fix it.
screen: `A SWINEHERD BOY, THEN A HERMIT.` · `A CHURCH SELLING ITS OFFICES.` · `BLUNT LETTERS, AND BLUNT WITH HIMSELF.` · `CALLED TO HELP, LONGING FOR HIS CELL.` · then, large: `BETTER ARE THE WOUNDS OF A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one corruption, gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing that's gone a little crooked: at work, in a group you belong to, in your own habits. A rule bent for friends. A small lie that's become normal. Name it, privately, in plain words, the way Peter Damian would. Then do what he did with his signature: find your own part in it, however small. Don't plan a speech. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can bring it to God and ask for the courage to say it kindly. If you don't, let it sit, named, while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Peter Damian. A hermit monk and reformer, later a cardinal and Doctor of the Church, who wrote hard letters out of love and called himself Peter the sinner.
Your line: blunt love. Today, if a hard thing needs saying, say it plainly and warmly, and say your own part first. Day nine hundred seventy.

971.title: Gregory of Narek (27 February)
971.hook: an Armenian monk whose Book of Lamentations is a conversation with God from the depths
971.howItsDone: Armenian Christians, both Apostolic and Catholic, honor Saint Gregory of Narek, and some families keep his Book of Lamentations at home for prayer, especially in illness; in the Roman calendar he is remembered on 27 February.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Damian, the monk who wrote hard letters to popes and signed himself a sinner. Your line was blunt love. Did a hard thing get said kindly? Day nine hundred seventy-one.

In some Armenian homes there's a book kept near the bed, or tucked under the pillow of someone who is sick. It isn't a medicine guide. It's a book of prayers, and people often call it simply by its author's village: the Narek. Tradition says families read from it at bedsides and in hard nights, the way others keep a rosary in a pocket. Its author was a monk who lived at a monastery called Narek, by a lake in Armenia, long ago. Today is about him, and about a book that starts from the bottom.
screen: `A BOOK UNDER THE PILLOW.` → `THEY CALL IT THE NAREK.` → `A MONK BY A LAKE.`

segments.voice: Gregory called his book a Book of Lamentations. Each of its prayers, by tradition, opens with the same phrase, which can be put in English as speaking with God from the depths of the heart. And he means the depths. Gregory doesn't write as a holy man explaining prayer to beginners. He writes as someone who has looked honestly at himself and doesn't like all of what he sees. He piles up images for his own brokenness: a ship breaking apart, a field gone to weeds, a debtor with nothing to pay. Page after page, he refuses to pretend. And then, again and again, he turns. Not to his own goodness, which he's just given up on, but to God's mercy, which he trusts more than his own despair. He even prays for the people who will read him, and for those who wrong him. If that shape sounds familiar, it's old. The Psalms have it. In the Douay-Rheims, the psalm Catholics know as the De profundis begins: "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." Gregory's book reads like that first line, carried across page after page. He belongs first to the Armenian Apostolic Church, which honors him as a saint. Armenian Catholics honor him too, and Pope Francis named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Catholic Church. A monk who wrote so honestly about how lost he was became a teacher. That might be the point. Prayer doesn't have to start from the top.
screen: `SPEAKING WITH GOD FROM THE DEPTHS.` · `HONEST ABOUT HIS OWN BROKENNESS.` · `THEN TURNING TO MERCY.` · `AN ARMENIAN DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS I HAVE CRIED TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray, or sit, from the depths. Settle, and breathe. Let one honest thing rise: something you're carrying that isn't tidy. A failure, a fear, a grudge, a tiredness. Don't dress it up and don't argue it down. Just let it be what it is. Then, the way Gregory does, turn. If you pray, you can say the first line of that psalm, out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord, and leave the rest to God. If you don't, breathe out slowly, and let the heavy thing sit beside you rather than on top of you. The bell holds the time.
Gregory of Narek. An Armenian monk whose Book of Lamentations speaks with God from the depths of the heart, and a Doctor of the Church.
Your line: the book of lamentations. Today, when something low comes up, don't skip past it. Name it honestly once, then turn toward whatever mercy you can find. Day nine hundred seventy-one.

972.title: Casimir (4 March)
972.hook: a young Polish prince who turned back from a war and gave to the poor
972.howItsDone: Catholics keep 4 March as the memorial of Saint Casimir, with special celebrations in Lithuania and Poland, where pilgrims visit his chapel in Vilnius cathedral and a traditional Kaziukas fair is held in Vilnius around his feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory of Narek, the Armenian monk who spoke with God from the depths of the heart. Your line was the book of lamentations. What did you name honestly? Day nine hundred seventy-two.

A young prince rides at the head of an army. His father, the king of Poland, has sent him to take a neighboring crown, the crown of Hungary, which some nobles there have offered him. Banners, horses, the whole weight of a dynasty behind him. And partway there, the prince turns around and goes home. Tradition gives more than one reason: soldiers deserting for lack of pay, a pope against the war, a rival king already holding the throne. But the Church remembers what the prince did with that moment. Today is about Casimir.
screen: `A YOUNG PRINCE AT THE HEAD OF AN ARMY.` → `A CROWN ON OFFER.` → `HE TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: The story goes that Casimir's father was furious and sent him away from court for a while. Casimir would not be talked into marching again. Whatever the full mix of reasons, his biographers tell it as a matter of conscience, and he never changed his mind. What he did instead is the part his biographers lingered on. He lived plainly inside a palace. Tradition says he slept on the floor, rose at night to pray at church doors before they opened, and gave his own money to the poor, the sick and pilgrims, so freely that he became known as their defender. He had a deep love for Mary, and tradition says he loved a Latin hymn that begins Omni die dic Mariae, daily, daily, sing to Mary, and that a copy was buried with him. He fell ill with a lung disease and died young, before he ever ruled anything. He is buried in the cathedral in Vilnius, and Lithuania and Poland both claim him as a patron. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says on the mountain: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Casimir was a king's son who chose to be remembered as one of those children instead. Refusing a fight is not always the easy road. For a prince, it meant his father's anger, a lost crown and a quiet life the court didn't understand.
screen: `A PRINCE WHO WON'T MARCH AGAIN.` · `PLAIN LIVING INSIDE A PALACE.` · `DAILY, DAILY, SING TO MARY.` · `A PATRON OF LITHUANIA AND POLAND.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: refuse a fight. Settle, and breathe. Find one fight you're in or about to be in: an argument you're rehearsing, a group chat you're ready to win, a family quarrel with your next line already written. Hold it up and ask whether this is one worth marching for. If it isn't, picture yourself turning the horse around. It might cost something: being right, the last word. Let it cost that. If you pray, you can ask God for the peace Jesus blesses. If you don't, breathe out slowly and set the next line down. The bell holds the time.
Casimir. A Polish prince who turned back from a war, gave to the poor, and died young, a patron of Lithuania and Poland.
Your line: the prince who refused. Today, when a fight offers itself, try turning it down once, and notice what you keep instead. Day nine hundred seventy-two.

973.title: John of God (8 March)
973.hook: a former soldier and bookseller who began caring for the sick, and whose followers became a hospital order
973.howItsDone: Catholics keep 8 March as the memorial of Saint John of God, patron of hospitals, nurses and the sick, and the Hospitaller Order he inspired runs hospitals and care homes that mark the day with Mass and celebrations for patients and staff.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Casimir, the prince who turned his army around and gave his money to the poor. Your line was the prince who refused. Which fight did you turn down? Day nine hundred seventy-three.

A street in Granada, in Spain. A man who sells holy books and pictures from a little shop stands in a crowd listening to the preacher John of Avila. Something in the sermon breaks him open. He runs through the streets shouting, crying out for mercy, tearing up his own books, giving away everything in the shop. The neighbors decide he has lost his mind. So he is taken to the city hospital and locked in the ward for the mad. That ward is where today's story really begins. His name was John, and the Church calls him John of God.
screen: `A BOOKSELLER IN GRANADA.` → `A SERMON BREAKS HIM OPEN.` → `LOCKED IN THE WARD FOR THE MAD.`

segments.voice: Before Granada, tradition says, John had been a shepherd, a soldier and a drifter. None of it had gone well. Now he was inside the hospital, and he saw what was done there to people judged insane. On that ward, tradition says, the treatment was beating, to drive the madness out. John was beaten too. And he made a decision, there on the ward: if he ever got out, he would care for the sick the way he wished someone had cared for him and the men beside him. John of Avila came to visit him and calmed him, and when John was released, he did exactly that. He rented a house, filled it with the sick and the homeless, and went out at night with a basket, begging for them. Tradition says his cry in the streets was, roughly, do good, brothers, to yourselves, meaning that helping the poor was a gift to the giver. He washed patients, carried them on his back, and sorted them by need. The bishop, tradition says, gave him the name John of God. After his death his helpers carried on, and became the Hospitaller Brothers of Saint John of God, a religious order devoted to the sick. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus describes the judgment, and the kindnesses done to him in the least of people: "sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me." John had been both. A man who had been treated as mad became a patron of hospitals and the sick.
screen: `SHEPHERD, SOLDIER, DRIFTER, BOOKSELLER.` · `BEATEN ON THE WARD FOR THE MAD.` · `A RENTED HOUSE AND A BASKET AT NIGHT.` · `HIS HELPERS BECOME AN ORDER.` · then, large: `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fill John's basket. Settle, and breathe. Picture him at night in Granada, going door to door with an empty basket for the sick in his rented house. Now bring to mind one person you know who is ill, or worn out caring for someone who is. Ask what would actually go in a basket for them. Not flowers. Soup. A lift to an appointment. Their bins taken out. An hour so the carer can sleep. Choose one thing and put it in the basket. If you pray, you can pray for that person and the people who care for them. If you don't, just keep them in mind with your breathing. The bell holds the time.
John of God. A soldier and bookseller, once locked up as mad, who began caring for the sick in Granada and whose helpers became the Hospitaller Brothers.
